docs.title: TimeLord
docs.text:
TimeLord tracks how Windows devices on your network are actually being used — who's logged in, for how long, and whether the machine is even reachable — shows it on a live dashboard, and can put devices to sleep or shut them down on a schedule you control, warning the person at the keyboard first.

Developer preview — not for production use

This is a working proof of the system's shape, not a hardened product. Expect rough edges and breaking changes between versions. Things worth knowing before you point it at real devices — details in Before you deploy this:

  • It acts on devices. A device with a schedule is put to sleep or shut down at its off times. Session limits, forced breaks and connectivity rules are not implemented — the project's tagline still describes the eventual product.
  • A device without a schedule is never slept or shut down. Only an assigned schedule acts on a device.
  • Every agent must reach the controller directly, on the same network(s). Everything is unicast HTTP — no NAT traversal, relay, or cloud/VPN routing.

It also runs over plain, unauthenticated HTTP — and that includes the admin API, so anyone who can reach the controller can send messages, grant extra time and delete devices. See Security boundary before running it anywhere but a trusted local network.

docs.title: What it actually does today
docs.text:
• Windows agent (Rust service) watches Windows session/power notifications — logon, lock, unlock, logoff, console/RDP connect and disconnect, suspend, resume — and the currently logged-in user (including one already logged in when the service starts), and reports them to a controller. Every event is queued to local disk before delivery, so a controller outage never loses data; queued events retry with backoff and flush immediately on reconnect or shutdown.
  • Controller (Java / Spring Boot / PostgreSQL) accepts registration, heartbeats, and events over HTTP, and shows each device as one of three states:
    • Offline — no events received within the timeout window.
    • Inactive — online (agent reachable, recent heartbeats), but nobody's logged in.
    • Active — online and a user is actually logged in right now.
  • Login sessions — a per-device history of login → logout spans, derived from the event log, distinct from "the agent was running." Starting the service with nobody logged in shows the machine online but produces no session at all.
  • Schedules — named weekly schedules of on-windows, several per day if you like (e.g. on 07:00–08:30 and 15:30–21:30 on school days), with dated overrides that add time for holidays and never modify the base schedule. The device is slept or shut down whenever it is outside every window. Assign a schedule to each device; the agent keeps enforcing from a local cache even if the controller is down. See Schedules.
  • Allow longer — one click (+15 / +30 / +60 minutes) lets a device stay on past its off time; the agent hears about it within moments via a long poll.
  • Notifier and messages — a small per-user program shows Windows toast warnings before a sleep or shutdown, and messages you send from the dashboard to one or all devices. See Notifier.
  • Dashboard — a server-rendered admin UI: device list with live status, per-device detail (network interfaces, current user, login history, schedule, messages), schedule management, a searchable event log, and device deletion.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text: The dashboard shows exactly one status badge per device — here Offline, Active   (online with someone logged in) and Locked — and a form to send a message to every device. Device detail — Session tab: live status, every network adapter (name/MAC/address),   and who's currently logged in. Device detail — History tab: every login session for this device, and how each one   ended (logged out, disappeared, and so on). Device detail — Service tab: the agent service's own state — registration and   heartbeat timestamps, independent of whether anyone's logged in. A schedule: weekly rows (several windows on the same day), dated overrides (half-term, a   sleepover, the Christmas holidays) that only ever add time, and the on-windows it resolves to over   the next 14 days. On a device: the assigned schedule, its upcoming off times, and one-click +15 / +30 /   +60 minute extensions (here, 30 minutes already granted).

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
TimeLord runs as two containers — postgres + controller — via docker compose:

$ cp .env.example .env        # edit TIMELORD_PUBLIC_URL to your LAN IP
$ docker compose up --build   # postgres + controller on :9099, discovery UDP on :45821

Open http://localhost:9099 for the dashboard, or:

$ curl http://localhost:9099/api/v1/system/info

docs.title: Try the agent against it (from a dev machine, any OS)
docs.text:
$ cd agent
$ TIMELORD_CONTROLLER_URL=http://localhost:9099 cargo run -- run
timelord-agent> logon
timelord-agent> lock
timelord-agent> quit

This registers a device, sends an AGENT_STARTED/USER_LOGON/... event trail, and a heartbeat — all visible on the dashboard within a few seconds. See Agent for what logon/lock/... actually mean (the dev backend's interactive REPL stands in for real Windows session notifications when not running on Windows).

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
Windows service (Rust) that tracks device usage and reports it to a TimeLord Controller.

Note

Unauthenticated plain HTTP to the controller. There is no session-limit or break enforcement yet. The agent does enforce a schedule assigned by the controller (sleep or shutdown at off times); a device with no schedule is never put to sleep or shut down. See Security boundary.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Tracks usage sessions locally — contiguous spans of time the device was actually being used, not just powered on (see Usage tracking below).
  2. Finds a controller: an explicit controller.url, or active UDP discovery.
  3. Registers, sends periodic heartbeats, and reports events (AGENT_STARTED, USER_LOGON, USER_LOCK, ... — the full list is in protocol.rs::EventType).
  4. Queues events locally (SQLite) so a controller outage never loses one — see Event delivery and idempotency.
  5. Receives its schedule as concrete off windows (in heartbeat responses and via a long poll that delivers changes within moments), caches it in schedule.json, and puts the device to sleep or shuts it down inside an off window — also while the controller is unreachable. At startup and after a sleep it first waits for the controller to confirm the cached schedule (up to 90 seconds), since a schedule edit or extension may have happened meanwhile; see Startup and resume.
  6. Long-polls for administrator messages, caches them in messages.json, and serves pending power actions and messages to the per-user notifier over a local named pipe (\\.\pipe\timelord-notify, read-only).

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
timelord-agent run                    Foreground, for development/debugging
timelord-agent service                Via the Windows SCM (what install registers)
timelord-agent install                Register + start the Windows service
timelord-agent uninstall              Stop + remove the Windows service
timelord-agent status                 Print resolved config + local queue size
timelord-agent discover [--force]     Run UDP discovery once, print results
                                       (--force also persists the winner to agent.toml)
timelord-agent test-event             Queue + attempt to deliver one synthetic event

run accepts --controller-url, --device-id, --device-name, --no-discovery to override agent.toml for that invocation only (see Configuration).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
C:\ProgramData\TimeLord\agent.toml (override the directory with TIMELORD_DATA_DIR):

[agent]
device_id = ""                       # generated + persisted on first run if empty
device_name = ""                     # defaults to the hostname if empty
heartbeat_interval_seconds = 30
event_retry_interval_seconds = 10

[controller]
url = ""                             # e.g. "http://192.168.1.20:8080"
discovery_enabled = true
discovery_port = 45821
discovery_timeout_seconds = 5

[time]
ntp_enabled = true                   # check the system clock against NTP; schedules use NTP time
ntp_servers = ["time.cloudflare.com", "time.windows.com", "pool.ntp.org"]   # the defaults

docs.title: The clock
docs.text:
A schedule is a list of absolute UTC times, so it is only as right as the time the agent compares it with, and Windows lets a user change the system clock. The agent therefore doesn't trust it: it measures the system clock against NTP servers (SNTP over UDP port 123) and enforces schedules, the notifier's countdowns and message expiry against NTP-corrected time.

  • It measures at startup, every 15 minutes, after any sleep, and whenever it sees the system clock jump (the system clock stops keeping pace with the agent's own timer). The median of the servers that answer is used, so one wrong server can't move it.
  • A system clock more than 30 seconds out is logged as a warning, for example the system clock is behind the real time; schedules use NTP time, with the offset in seconds.
  • At startup a cached schedule isn't enforced until the clock has been checked as well as the schedule confirmed by the controller, or until the 90-second grace period passes if NTP can't be reached.
  • If NTP becomes unreachable the last measured offset is kept, so blocking NTP only freezes the last measurement; a clock changed afterwards is still caught by the jump check once NTP is reachable again. The agent needs outbound UDP 123 (or your own server in ntp_servers).
  • ntp_enabled = false switches this off and uses the system clock. timelord-agent status shows which servers are configured.

Event timestamps sent to the controller still use the system clock.

docs.title: Devices without a schedule
docs.text:
A device with no schedule assigned is unrestricted: the agent never puts it to sleep or shuts it down. Earlier versions slept such a device 02:00–06:00 and, while the controller was unreachable, 01:00–08:30. Both are gone, and any offline_fallback_* keys left in agent.toml are ignored.

An assigned schedule keeps being enforced from the agent's cached copy while the controller is unreachable, so losing the network doesn't lift it.

Precedence is CLI flags > environment variables > agent.toml > defaults, unit tested for every combination. Environment overrides:

TIMELORD_CONTROLLER_URL
TIMELORD_DEVICE_ID
TIMELORD_DEVICE_NAME
TIMELORD_DISCOVERY_ENABLED

A discovered controller URL is persisted back to agent.toml; a manually-configured URL is never silently overwritten (only discover --force does that, since running it is itself the explicit request).

docs.title: Usage tracking
docs.text:
A service running as LocalSystem lives in Windows Session 0, isolated from the interactive desktop, so it can't just poll keyboard/mouse activity. Instead it relies on real-time OS notifications:

  • WTSRegisterSessionNotification (registered with NOTIFY_FOR_ALL_SESSIONS) delivers WM_WTSSESSION_CHANGE for logon, logoff, lock, unlock, console connect/disconnect, and RDP connect/disconnect — for every session, even from Session 0.
  • RegisterSuspendResumeNotification delivers suspend/resume via WM_POWERBROADCAST, so sleeping time isn't counted as usage.
  • True idle-while-unlocked detection (GetLastInputInfo) is per-desktop and unreachable from a Session-0 service. That needs a small per-user companion process reporting idle time back over a local IPC channel — not implemented yet; heartbeats currently send idleSeconds: null.

A usage session is therefore: logged on, unlocked, visible (console or RDP), and not suspended. A second session keeps the device "active" while a first one locks; resume alone only restarts a session if it never locked before suspend.

Every tracker notification also becomes a reported event (USER_LOGON, USER_LOCK, SYSTEM_SUSPEND, etc.) independent of whether it changed local usage-session state. Derived activity transitions are separate first-class ACTIVE/INACTIVE events, so a real logon may appear as USER_LOGON, ACTIVE; startup reconciliation of an already logged-in session does not create a synthetic logon.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
By default state lives under C:\ProgramData\TimeLord\ (override with TIMELORD_DATA_DIR):

state.db        Usage sessions
events.db       Local event queue pending controller delivery
agent.toml      Configuration
schedule.json   Cached schedule (resolved off windows); absent if no schedule
messages.json   Cached administrator messages and the polling cursor
logs/           Daily-rolling structured logs

If the agent is killed rather than shut down cleanly, the next start finds any dangling open usage session and closes it with end_reason = AGENT_RESTART, and resumes delivering whatever was still queued in events.db — nothing is lost.

docs.title: Running on Windows
docs.text:
> timelord-agent.exe install       # register as a LocalSystem service and start it
> timelord-agent.exe status
> timelord-agent.exe uninstall

install/uninstall use the Service Control Manager API directly, not sc.exe. A packaged zip with a PowerShell installer is attached to every tagged release on GitHub. To install from it, extract the zip and run, from PowerShell as Administrator in that folder:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
.\install.ps1

Why the first line

Windows blocks PowerShell scripts that came from a download by default. -Scope Process lifts that for the current PowerShell window only; nothing is changed permanently, and it reverts when you close the window. Alternatively run Unblock-File .\install.ps1, .\uninstall.ps1 (or untick Unblock in the zip's Properties before extracting). Re-running install.ps1 with a newer timelord-agent.exe upgrades an existing install.

The zip contains both timelord-agent.exe and timelord-notifier.exe, and install.ps1 also registers a TimeLord Notifier scheduled task that starts the notifier at each user's logon (-SkipNotifier to skip it).

docs.title: TimeLord Architecture
docs.text:
This is a developer preview, not a product. It exists to prove the shape of the system on a single trusted local network. It has not been hardened, load-tested, or run unattended for long periods, there are no stability guarantees between versions, and it is not meant for production use. See Before you deploy this below.

It monitors, and it enforces schedules. Beyond reporting what each device is doing, a device assigned a schedule is put to sleep or shut down at its off times, with on-screen warnings from a per-user notifier and admin messages. There is still no session-limit enforcement, mandatory-break logic, connectivity rules, or immediate remote power commands. See What's implemented below.

It is also deliberately unsecured. Plain HTTP, no authentication, no request signing, no access control — including on the admin API that manages schedules, sends messages and deletes devices. It exists to prove the shape of the system on a trusted local network, ahead of a later security phase. See Security boundary below before running this anywhere else.

docs.title: Before you deploy this
docs.text:
• Developer preview. Expect rough edges, breaking config/schema changes between versions, and no migration tooling. Test on a couple of non-critical machines before trusting it with anything that matters.
  • Every agent must be able to reach the controller directly, on the same network(s). All traffic — registration, heartbeats, event delivery, and discovery replies — is unicast HTTP (broadcast UDP only for the initial discovery request). There's no NAT traversal, no relay, and no cloud/VPN-aware routing: if an agent's machine can't open a TCP connection straight to TIMELORD_PUBLIC_URL, it can't be managed at all. See Known limitations for the additional constraint this puts on UDP discovery specifically (same broadcast domain, not just same routed network).
  • A device with no schedule is unrestricted. Earlier versions slept such a device 02:00–06:00, and 01:00–08:30 while the controller was unreachable; both rules were removed. Only an assigned schedule ever puts a device to sleep or shuts it down.
  • A schedule sleeps or shuts the device down. At its off times a device with a schedule is suspended or powered off (shutdown.exe /s /t 30, a 30-second warning). Test on a spare machine first; the agent-side actions are covered by unit tests and compile checks only.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
TimeLord has four moving pieces:

  • TimeLord Agent (Rust) — runs on each Windows device as a service. Tracks when the device is actually in use (not just powered on — see agent/README.md), who's logged in, and every network adapter (name/MAC/ address). Finds a controller (explicit URL or UDP discovery), registers, and reports usage/lifecycle events and heartbeats. Caches its schedule and enforces it (sleep or shutdown), and serves a local pipe to the notifier.
  • TimeLord Notifier (Rust) — a small program that runs in each logged-on user's session, polls the agent over a local pipe, and shows toast warnings before a sleep/shutdown plus administrator messages.
  • TimeLord Controller (Java 21 / Spring Boot) — the single source of truth. Accepts registration/heartbeats/events over HTTP, listens for UDP discovery requests, persists everything to PostgreSQL, computes each device's status, resolves schedules into off windows, queues messages, and serves both the REST API and a server-rendered (Thymeleaf) admin dashboard.
  • PostgreSQL — durable storage for devices, events, heartbeats, schedules, and messages.

The agent never loses an event to a controller outage: every event is written to a local SQLite queue before any delivery attempt, and only removed once the controller acknowledges it (including an acknowledged duplicate, which counts as delivered). Time-sensitive events (agent shutdown, reconnecting after being offline) flush immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled retry.

docs.title: What's implemented
docs.text:
• Device registration, heartbeats, event ingestion over the HTTP API, with idempotent event submission (see Event delivery and idempotency).
  • Two independent statuses per device, shown on the dashboard:
    • Online / Offline — is the agent reachable (heartbeat recency)?
    • Active — is a user actually logged in right now (Device.isActive() — online and a current user reported over heartbeat)?
  • Login sessions — a per-device history of login → logout spans (DeviceSessionService), reconstructed at read time from USER_LOGON / USER_LOGOFF / AGENT_STOPPING / SYSTEM_SUSPEND / HEARTBEAT_SENT events rather than stored in a separate table. A device that's merely online with nobody logged in — including right after the agent starts — has no session at all; only an actual logon starts one, and logoff, agent shutdown, suspend, or the agent going silent for too long ends it.
  • Activity history — ACTIVE and INACTIVE are persisted separately from session events. A real logon can therefore produce USER_LOGON followed by ACTIVE; startup reconciliation does not produce a synthetic logon.
  • Network interface inventory — every adapter the OS reports (not just ones with a routable address), with name, MAC, and address(es), shown on the device detail page.
  • Schedules — named weekly on-windows (any number per day) with dated overrides that only add time, assigned to devices. The controller resolves a schedule into concrete off windows (applying any extension) and sends them to the agent with a revision; the agent caches them in schedule.json and sleeps or shuts the device down inside a window, even offline. See Schedules.
  • Extensions — a per-device "allow longer" grant (+15/30/60 min) that delays the next off window without touching the schedule.
  • Push-style change delivery — the agent long-polls the controller for schedule changes and messages, so an extension or a message takes effect in moments, not at the next heartbeat.
  • Messages — free-text messages from the dashboard to one or all devices, stored with a per-device cursor and delivered when the device is (back) online, until they expire.
  • Notifier — a per-user program that polls the agent over a local named pipe and shows toast warnings before a sleep/shutdown and any messages. See Notifier.
  • Admin dashboard — device list with live status, per-device detail (including schedule, extension and messages), schedule management, a searchable/filterable event log, and device deletion (removes the device's events, heartbeats and messages; a still-running agent simply registers again).

Not implemented: session-limit enforcement, mandatory breaks, connectivity requirements, immediate remote power commands (the only remote action is granting more time), a countdown window or tray icon in the notifier, or any policy engine beyond schedules — despite what the root README's tagline aspires to.

docs.title: Discovery sequence
docs.text:
Active discovery (the primary mechanism) vs. the explicit-URL path both feed into the same registration flow:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant Controller

    alt controller.url configured
        Agent->>Agent: use configured URL directly
    else no URL configured
        Agent->>Controller: UDP broadcast DISCOVER_CONTROLLER (requestId)
        Controller-->>Agent: UDP unicast CONTROLLER_AVAILABLE (same requestId)
        Note over Agent: validate protocol/version/requestId/URL, if multiple replies, pick by priority, then speed, then smallest controller ID
        Agent->>Agent: persist chosen URL to agent.toml
    end

    Agent->>Controller: POST /api/v1/agents/register
    Controller-->>Agent: 200 { deviceId, controllerId, heartbeatIntervalSeconds }
    loop every heartbeatIntervalSeconds
        Agent->>Controller: POST /api/v1/agents/{deviceId}/heartbeat
    end
    loop every eventRetryIntervalSeconds
        Agent->>Controller: POST /api/v1/agents/{deviceId}/events (batch)
        Controller-->>Agent: ACCEPTED / DUPLICATE / REJECTED per event
    end

UDP broadcast only reaches devices in the same broadcast domain, and Docker's bridge network typically doesn't forward broadcast traffic to a published UDP port at all — see Known limitations. The explicit controller.url path always works and is what .env.example sets up by default.

docs.title: Schedule and message delivery
docs.text:
Schedules and messages reach an agent two ways, and the second is what makes changes take effect quickly:

  • Heartbeat responses (and registration) carry the device's current schedule, resolved to concrete off windows for the next 28 days plus a revision that changes whenever they do.
  • Long polls. The agent keeps GET /api/v1/agents/{id}/schedule?revision=… and GET /api/v1/agents/{id}/messages?after=<seq> open for up to ~30 seconds each (own connections, so they never block heartbeats). The controller answers the moment the revision differs or a message is queued for that device — an extension, assignment, schedule edit or new message — and otherwise returns after the timeout so the agent asks again.

The agent caches both (schedule.json, messages.json) and keeps enforcing from the cache while the controller is unreachable. Because that cache can be stale after the device has been off or asleep, the agent re-confirms it with the controller on startup and after a sleep before enforcing it (falling back to the cache after 90 seconds without an answer). The notifier then reads that cache through the agent's local pipe; see Notifier.

docs.title: Event delivery and idempotency
docs.text:
• Every event gets a client-generated eventId (UUID). The controller uses it as the primary key of device_event, so retransmitting the same event is safe: the second submission is reported as DUPLICATE, not inserted again.
  • The agent's local queue (events.db) treats DUPLICATE the same as ACCEPTED — both remove the event from the local queue.
  • A failed submission schedules a retry with bounded backoff (10s, 30s, 1m, 5m, 15m, 30m, holding at 30m), and an event that fails MAX_ATTEMPTS times is discarded rather than retried forever.

docs.title: Security boundary
docs.text:
This phase intentionally has:

  • No TLS (plain http://)
  • No authentication of agents or administrators
  • No request signing or replay protection
  • No access control on any endpoint — including the admin endpoints that create/edit schedules, assign them, grant extensions, send messages and delete devices. Anyone who can reach the controller can do all of that.

The one local control is the agent's notifier pipe: its access list lets SYSTEM and Administrators do anything and lets ordinary users read and write data only (no creating pipe instances), and it refuses remote clients. The pipe is read-only — a user can ask what is pending but cannot change anything through it.

Only run this on an isolated or trusted local network. The code is structured so a later phase can add HTTPS, controller-key pinning, Ed25519 agent identity, signed events, and role-based admin access without rewriting the event model:

  • Controller: AgentRequestAuthenticator (common/AgentRequestAuthenticator.java) — ships only NoOpAgentRequestAuthenticator.
  • Agent: RequestSigner trait (controller_client.rs) — ships only NoOpRequestSigner.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Docker + UDP broadcast: a Windows agent on the LAN broadcasting to 255.255.255.255:45821 generally will not reach a controller published from inside Docker's default bridge network — Docker's NAT forwards packets addressed to the host's specific IP, not to the broadcast address. Use the explicit controller.url (Mode A) for anything beyond same-host experimentation, or run the controller directly on the host for discovery testing. TIMELORD_PUBLIC_URL must be a LAN-reachable address, never the in-Docker hostname controller.
  • TIMELORD_PUBLIC_URL is what gets handed to agents during discovery and registration responses; it must be reachable from agent devices, which .env.example calls out.
  • OS version detection is a placeholder (agent_version/architecture are real; operatingSystemVersion is not populated yet) — see agent.rs::os_info.
  • No persisted device_session table yet — EventItem.sessionId is always null; the OS-level Windows session ID is carried in data.windowsSessionId instead. The dashboard's "User sessions" list (see What's implemented) is reconstructed at read time from the event log by DeviceSessionService, not backed by a session table — that's still a later phase.
  • Login sessions are single-user-at-a-time per device — the agent caches one username per Windows session ID, but the controller's session/active model doesn't distinguish concurrent logons (fast user switching, RDP).
  • No idle-time detection — a Session-0 service can't call GetLastInputInfo for the interactive desktop; heartbeats currently send idleSeconds: null. The per-user notifier is the natural home for this but doesn't report idle time yet. See agent/README.md.
  • Schedules wake nothing. "On" means allowed to be on; a sleeping device stays asleep until someone wakes it (there is no Wake-on-LAN).
  • Enforcement is only unit-tested. The agent's sleep/shutdown and the notifier's toasts compile for Windows and their logic is tested, but they have not been run end to end on real machines.
  • Message "delivered" is not "seen" — the controller records when it handed a message to the agent, not whether the user saw it.
  • The agent's message cursor is a database sequence. If the controller database is reset, an agent holding a higher cursor will miss new messages until its messages.json is deleted.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text: Central controller service (Java 21 / Spring Boot / PostgreSQL). Accepts agent registration, heartbeats, and events over plain HTTP (unauthenticated — see Security boundary), resolves schedules into off windows, queues messages, and serves a Thymeleaf admin dashboard.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
The normal path is docker compose up --build from the repo root — see Get started.

Tagged releases (timelord-vX.Y.Z) also publish a pre-built image to GHCR, so compose.yaml doesn't have to build from source:

$ docker pull ghcr.io/johnjoeallen/timelord-controller:X.Y.Z   # or :latest for the newest release

To run just the controller against a local Postgres:

$ docker run -d --name timelord-postgres -p 5432:5432 \
    -e POSTGRES_DB=timelord -e POSTGRES_USER=timelord -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=timelord postgres:17
$ mvn spring-boot:run

Config is environment-driven (application.yml); the important ones:

SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL / _USERNAME / _PASSWORD
TIMELORD_CONTROLLER_NAME
TIMELORD_PUBLIC_URL           # must be reachable by agents — never the Docker-internal hostname
TIMELORD_DISCOVERY_ENABLED / _PORT / _PRIORITY
TIMELORD_ANNOUNCEMENT_ENABLED / _INTERVAL
TIMELORD_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_SECONDS
TIMELORD_HEARTBEAT_RETENTION_DAYS

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
src/main/java/com/timelord/controller/
├── config/     @ConfigurationProperties records (controller/discovery/device/heartbeat)
├── agent/      Agent-facing DTOs + AgentController (register/heartbeat/events)
├── device/     Device entity/repository/service, admin DeviceController, online/offline
│               scheduler, DeviceSessionService (login-session reconstruction)
├── event/      DeviceEvent/DeviceHeartbeat entities, EventService (idempotent submission),
│               admin EventController, heartbeat retention scheduler
├── discovery/  UDP listener + optional periodic announcer, controller identity persistence
├── calendar/   Calendar/rule/override entities, CalendarResolver (rules + overrides -> off
│               windows), CalendarService, admin CalendarController
├── message/    DeviceMessage entity, MessageService, admin MessageController,
│               MessageChangeNotifier (wakes message long polls)
├── dashboard/  Thymeleaf DashboardController + CalendarDashboardController (form posts)
├── health/     Custom actuator health indicator (discovery listener)
└── common/     ApiError/ApiException/GlobalExceptionHandler, correlation IDs,
                AgentRequestAuthenticator (no-op — the Phase-2 auth seam)

Flyway migrations: src/main/resources/db/migration/. Templates: src/main/resources/templates/.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/system/info · admin: /api/v1/devices, /api/v1/devices/{id}, DELETE /api/v1/devices/{id} (also removes its events, heartbeats and messages), /api/v1/devices/{id}/events, /api/v1/events, /api/v1/events/{id}, plus /api/v1/calendars/**, PUT /api/v1/devices/{id}/calendar, POST /api/v1/devices/{id}/extend and /api/v1/devices/{id}/messages, POST /api/v1/messages (see Schedules and Notifier) · agent: /api/v1/agents/register, /api/v1/agents/{id}/heartbeat, /api/v1/agents/{id}/events, and the long polls GET /api/v1/agents/{id}/schedule and GET /api/v1/agents/{id}/messages.

Heartbeat and registration responses also carry the device's resolved schedule (schedule, null without a schedule).

Errors are a consistent JSON shape (timestamp/status/code/message/details/correlationId); device/event lookups return 404 with code DEVICE_NOT_FOUND / EVENT_NOT_FOUND.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: / (dashboard, with a "message all devices" form), /devices (filterable list), /devices/{id} (detail, login session history, schedule assignment and "allow longer" buttons, send-a-message with history, delete device), /calendars and /calendars/{id} (create and edit schedules, weekly rules, overrides, 14-day preview), /events (filterable, paginated). Bootstrap is bundled via WebJars — no external CDN.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
$ mvn test

Integration tests use Testcontainers Postgres via a singleton container pattern — one Postgres for the whole test JVM, started once in a static initializer, not via @Container/@Testcontainers (that combination, with the field declared in a shared abstract base class, ties container start/stop to whichever subclass runs, which stops a still-referenced container out from under another test class's cached Spring context).

Running via Docker (no local Maven/JDK 21 needed), with the host Docker socket mounted so Testcontainers can start Postgres as a sibling container:

$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/build -w /build -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    -v timelord-maven-repo:/root/.m2 -e TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true \
    maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 mvn -B test

docs.title: Notifier and messages
docs.text:
The notifier is a small per-user program that gives the person at the keyboard notice of what the device is about to do, and shows messages sent by an administrator. It runs in each logged-on user's own session; the agent service still does all enforcement, so the schedule applies whether or not the notifier is running. The notifier only provides warning.

Developer preview

The notifier is new, has had unit tests and Windows compile checks but no field testing, and still lacks a last-minute countdown window and a tray icon (see Limitations).

docs.title: What the user sees
docs.text:
Warnings before sleep or shutdown. As an off time approaches (from a schedule), a Windows toast appears at 15 minutes, 5 minutes, 1 minute and 30 seconds, e.g. "This computer will go to sleep in 5 minutes — Scheduled: go to sleep at 22:30. Save your work."

  • Each tighter warning replaces the looser one in place rather than stacking.
  • The 1-minute and 30-second warnings use the Windows reminder scenario, so they stay on screen until dismissed.
  • If the notifier starts with 3 minutes left it shows the 5-minute warning, not also the 15.
  • If the action is cancelled or moved — for example you press +30 min on the device page — the toast is removed, and a new warning follows for the new time.

Messages. Anything sent from the dashboard appears as a toast with the title you gave (or "TimeLord"). Each message is shown once; the notifier remembers which it has shown, per user, so a restart or a later logon does not repeat them.

docs.title: Sending a message
docs.text:
Sending a message to one device, with the history showing one waiting and one delivered message. The dashboard has the same form for all devices.

From a device's page use Send a message, or from the dashboard use Message all devices.

Field Notes Title Optional, up to 100 characters Message Required, up to 500 characters Show for How long the message stays deliverable: 15 minutes, 1 hour, 4 hours (default) or 24 hours

A message to an offline device is held and delivered when the device reconnects, as long as it has not expired. The device page lists the last 10 messages as waiting, delivered or expired. Delivered means the controller handed it to the agent; it does not mean the user has seen it.

=== "One device"

```console
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:9099/api/v1/devices/$DEVICE_ID/messages \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"title": "Dinner", "body": "Ready in 10 minutes", "expiresInMinutes": 60}'
```

=== "Every device"

```console
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:9099/api/v1/messages \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"body": "Lights out at 22:30 tonight", "expiresInMinutes": 240}'
```

GET /api/v1/devices/{id}/messages lists a device's recent messages. expiresInMinutes may be 1 to 10080 (7 days). Like the rest of the admin API these endpoints are unauthenticated in this preview — see the security boundary.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Controller] -- "long poll: schedule, messages" --> A[Agent service]
    A -- "schedule.json / messages.json" --> D[(Local cache)]
    N[Notifier] -- "named pipe: GetPending / GetMessages" --> A
    N --> T[Windows toasts]
  • The agent long-polls the controller for messages with a cursor (seq), the same push-style mechanism it uses for schedule changes, and caches them in messages.json next to schedule.json. A message is never fetched twice and survives restarts.
  • The notifier asks the agent over a local named pipe, \\.\pipe\timelord-notify, using one JSON line per request and response. Two requests exist: GetPending (power actions starting in the next 30 minutes) and GetMessages (unexpired messages). The service is a passive, read-only responder and recomputes each answer from its current cache, so cancellations and extensions show up on the next poll. All timing and toast logic lives in the notifier.
  • The notifier polls every 10 seconds, and every 2 seconds in the last 90 seconds before an action. It judges remaining time against the service's clock, so a wrong clock on the user's account does not shift the warnings.
  • The pipe's access control lets SYSTEM and Administrators do anything and lets ordinary users read and write data only. In particular, users cannot create another instance of the pipe, so they cannot impersonate the service to other users.
  • Toasts need an app identity; the notifier registers TimeLord.Notifier under HKCU\Software\Classes\AppUserModelId for the current user (no administrator rights needed).

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
install.ps1 in the release zip installs the notifier and a TimeLord Notifier scheduled task that starts it at every user's logon (as that user, with limited rights, restarting on failure, one instance per session). Pass -SkipNotifier to install only the service. See Running on Windows and deployment/windows/README.md.

Per-user files live under %LOCALAPPDATA%\TimeLord:

notifier.log             Problems (the notifier has no console); rotated at 256 KiB
notifier-shown.json      Ids of messages already shown to this user

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No countdown window for the last minute and no tray icon yet; toasts are the only display, and Windows Focus Assist can suppress ordinary toasts (reminder-scenario ones fare better).
  • No postponing from the notifier — the only way to grant more time is the controller's +15 / +30 / +60 min buttons.
  • "Delivered" is not "seen": the notifier does not report back to the service or controller.
  • Windows only; there is nothing to talk to on other systems.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
A schedule tells a device when it may be on. You create named schedules in the dashboard, assign each device to one, and the agent puts the device to sleep (or shuts it down) whenever the schedule says it should be off — that is, outside every on-window. Nothing wakes a sleeping device: "on" only means allowed to be on.

The Schedules page: each schedule's action, timezone and how many weekly rows and overrides it has.

Developer preview

Scheduling is new. The agent-side sleep and shutdown have not been exercised on real hardware beyond compile checks and unit tests — try it on a spare machine first (see Trying it safely).

The schedule editor: weekly rows (several on the same day), overrides that add time, and the resolved on-windows for the next 14 days.

docs.title: How a schedule works
docs.text:
A schedule has a name, a timezone, and an action taken at off time:

Action What the agent does SLEEP Suspends the device (SetSuspendState, never hibernate) and keeps re-suspending it for as long as the schedule says off, if someone wakes it. SHUTDOWN Runs shutdown.exe /s /t 30 — a 30-second on-screen warning, then power off.

docs.title: Weekly rows (the base schedule)
docs.text:
Each day is its own line from midnight to midnight. A row has a set of days, an On from time and an Off at time, and says: on each of these days the device may be on from On from until Off at. You can add as many rows as you like, including several for the same day. All the windows are combined; the device is on inside them and off everywhere else.

Days On from Off at Meaning Mon–Fri 08:30 10:30 On 08:30–10:30 ... Mon–Fri 18:30 23:30 ... and again 18:30–23:30; off the rest of the day Sat, Sun (blank) (blank) The whole day Thu 00:00 16:15 On from midnight until 16:15 ... Thu 16:30 00:00 ... off 16:15–16:30, on again 16:30 until midnight

Rules for the times:

  • Windows stay inside their day. A window never runs past midnight; Off at 00:00 means midnight at the end of the day, so 18:30 → 00:00 is the evening and 00:00 → 00:00 is the whole day. Off at must otherwise be later than On from, and the dashboard and API refuse a row that isn't.
  • Blank means the edge of the day. Leave On from blank to start at the beginning of the day (00:00) and Off at blank to run to midnight; both blank is the whole day.
  • The next day takes over. A window that ends at midnight simply continues into the next day's window if that starts at 00:00 — there is no gap at midnight. So a late night is two rows: Fri, on from 18:00, no off and Sat, no on from, off at 01:00 give one continuous window from Friday 18:00 to Saturday 01:00.
  • Off for a while inside a day is a gap between two rows (the Thursday example above).
  • A day with no row is off all day — but a schedule with no rows at all restricts nothing, so a newly created, still-empty schedule doesn't keep a device asleep.

Rows are managed with the + and − buttons on the schedule page:

  • The bottom row is always blank. Fill it in and press + to keep it and get a new blank row; with nothing filled in, + does nothing.
  • − disables a row: it is dimmed, kept, and ignored (it gives no window, exactly as if it were deleted), so you can switch a row off and bring it back later. Pressing − on a disabled row deletes it.
  • Nothing is stored until you press Save schedule. A schedule whose rows are all disabled restricts nothing, like one with no rows.

Each row on the schedule page shows its next window (for example Next: Thu 22 Oct 18:30 → Thu 22 Oct 23:30), and the page lists the combined on-windows for the next 14 days, so you can check what a schedule does before relying on it.

Earlier versions

Earlier versions described a schedule as off times (one rule per day, an off and an on time, with an inferred "after midnight"). On upgrade the controller converts existing schedules to on-windows automatically: weekly rules become the equivalent rows exactly. Overrides are converted too, but they can no longer narrow a day (see below). A schedule whose old rules left no on-time at all ends up with no rows, which restricts nothing.

docs.title: Overrides (holidays and one-offs)
docs.text:
An override is a date range with an On from and an Off at time, written like a row (same blank and midnight rules). It is layered on after the weekly rows are expanded: for every date in the range it adds that window to the day, and everything is combined. So an override can extend a day or add time on a day with no row, but it can never narrow one — an override inside an existing window changes nothing. The weekly rows themselves are never edited; remove the override and the day goes back. A single day is an override whose start and end date are the same (in the dashboard, leave "To" blank). Overrides stack.

Example

Weekdays normally have 07:00–08:30 and 15:30–21:30. Half-term, 30 Oct – 8 Nov, on 09:00–23:00 adds a long window each of those days, so the device is on 07:00–08:30 and 09:00–23:00 (the window 15:30–21:30 is absorbed). Birthday sleepover, 13 Nov, on from 15:30 extends that evening to midnight, and a second override for 14 Nov, off at 02:00 (no on from) carries it to 02:00. To let a holiday run late you add the early-hours piece as an override for the next date.

docs.title: Allowing a device longer
docs.text:
The device page: schedule assignment, upcoming off times and the extension buttons.

On a device's page, +15 min / +30 min / +1 hour grant a temporary extension:

  • If the device is already inside an off window, it is allowed back on for that long from now.
  • Otherwise the next off window starts that much later.
  • Each request may grant 1–240 minutes; the page shows "Extended until HH:MM" with a Clear button.

An extension never edits the schedule. It is cleared if you assign the device a different schedule.

docs.title: How the device enforces it
docs.text:
The controller resolves the schedule (rows, overrides and any extension) into concrete off windows — the gaps between the on-windows, as absolute start and end times for the next 28 days — and sends them to the agent with a revision that changes whenever they do. The agent therefore never has to understand rows or overrides; it only asks whether the time now falls inside an off window.

  • Cached locally. The latest schedule is saved as schedule.json next to agent.toml, so enforcement continues across restarts and while the controller is unreachable.
  • Startup and resume. The cached schedule can be stale: the schedule may have been edited, or the device granted more time, while it was off or asleep. So the agent does not enforce the cache the moment it starts. It waits until the controller has confirmed the schedule (in the registration or heartbeat response, or a long poll). If the controller stays unreachable for 90 seconds it enforces the cache anyway, so an offline device is still governed. The same re-confirmation happens after the agent resumes from a sleep it caused, and after any wake it notices (a wake-up much later than planned, such as a closed lid). The notifier is not told about upcoming actions from an unconfirmed cache either. In practice a device that boots inside a cached off window stays on for a few seconds while it checks in, then either goes back to sleep (nothing changed) or stays on (the schedule or an extension now says it may).
  • Changes arrive immediately. Besides every heartbeat, the agent holds a long poll open to GET /api/v1/agents/{id}/schedule?revision=…. The controller answers the moment an extension, assignment or schedule edit changes the revision, so "+30 minutes" takes effect within moments, not at the next heartbeat. With no change the request simply returns after about 30 seconds and the agent asks again.
  • Trusted time. The agent compares the windows with NTP-corrected time, not the system clock, so changing the PC's clock doesn't move the schedule (see the clock).
  • Enforcement loop. The agent acts when the current time is inside an off window, and re-checks at the next window start, on any schedule change, and at least every 60 seconds — so a device woken mid-window is put back to sleep within about a minute. Each action is reported as POWER_ACTION_REQUESTED / _COMPLETED / _FAILED events.

docs.title: Devices without a schedule
docs.text: A device with no schedule assigned is unrestricted: the agent never puts it to sleep or shuts it down. Earlier versions slept such a device 02:00–06:00 (and 01:00–08:30 while the controller was unreachable); both rules were removed.

docs.title: Admin API
docs.text:
All of these are unauthenticated in this preview — see the security boundary.

Method and path Purpose GET /api/v1/calendars · GET /api/v1/calendars/{id} List / read schedules (with rows and overrides) POST /api/v1/calendars Create PUT /api/v1/calendars/{id} Replace name, timezone, action and the whole set of weekly rows (overrides untouched) DELETE /api/v1/calendars/{id} Delete; devices using it lose their schedule POST /api/v1/calendars/{id}/overrides Add an override DELETE /api/v1/calendars/{id}/overrides/{overrideId} Remove an override GET /api/v1/calendars/{id}/allowed?from=&days= Preview the resolved on-windows (what the dashboard's table shows) GET /api/v1/calendars/{id}/windows?from=&days= Preview the resolved off windows (what the agent is sent) PUT /api/v1/devices/{id}/calendar Assign ({"calendarId": "<uuid>"}) or clear ({"calendarId": null}) POST /api/v1/devices/{id}/extend Allow longer ({"minutes": 30}) GET /api/v1/agents/{id}/schedule Agent long poll for schedule changes (204 = no schedule)

=== "Create a schedule"

The JSON field for a row is still called `rules`; `startTime` / `endTime` may be left out
(start or end of the day), and `00:00` as an end means midnight. `"enabled": false` keeps a row
but ignores it (default `true`).

```console
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:9099/api/v1/calendars \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
      "name": "School days",
      "timezone": "Europe/Dublin",
      "action": "SLEEP",
      "rules": [
        {"days": ["MONDAY","TUESDAY","WEDNESDAY","THURSDAY","FRIDAY"], "startTime": "07:00", "endTime": "08:30"},
        {"days": ["MONDAY","TUESDAY","WEDNESDAY","THURSDAY","FRIDAY"], "startTime": "15:30", "endTime": "21:30"},
        {"days": ["SATURDAY","SUNDAY"], "startTime": "08:30", "endTime": "12:00"},
        {"days": ["SATURDAY","SUNDAY"], "startTime": "14:00"},
        {"days": ["SATURDAY","SUNDAY"], "endTime": "01:00"}
      ]
    }'
```

=== "Add a holiday override"

```console
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:9099/api/v1/calendars/$CALENDAR_ID/overrides \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
      "name": "Christmas",
      "startDate": "2026-12-19",
      "endDate": "2027-01-05",
      "startTime": "08:00"
    }'
```

=== "Another 30 minutes"

```console
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:9099/api/v1/devices/$DEVICE_ID/extend \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"minutes": 30}'
```

Validation errors come back in the usual error shape, for example INVALID_TIMEZONE, INVALID_RULE (no days, or an Off at that is not after On from — a window can't run past midnight, add a row for the next day), INVALID_OVERRIDE (the same, or an end date before the start date), CALENDAR_NAME_TAKEN (409), and NO_CALENDAR / NO_OFF_WINDOW (409) when extending a device that has nothing to extend.

docs.title: Trying it safely
docs.text:
1. Create a schedule with a window that ends about 20 minutes from now (say, on from blank, off at 20 minutes ahead, for today's weekday) and the Sleep action, and assign it to a spare device. Remember the rest of that day, and every other day without a row, is then off.
  2. Watch the device sleep at the end of the window; wake it and confirm it is put back to sleep.
  3. Assign it again, press +15 min shortly before the window ends, and confirm it stays on.
  4. Only then try Shutdown, again on a machine you can afford to power off.
